title: Tennessee Seller Disclosure: Condition Form and Lead Paint
description: A plain-spoken look at the Tennessee seller disclosure: the residential property condition disclosure, the 1978 lead-based paint rule.
body:
Before your home goes on the market, there is paperwork that has nothing to do with staging or photos. In Tennessee, the seller disclosure is part of that paperwork, and it is easier to handle before you have an offer than in the middle of one.

This post explains the two disclosures sellers hear about most: the residential property condition disclosure and the lead-based paint disclosure for older homes. I am not an attorney, so treat this as a plain-language overview and not legal advice.

## The Tennessee seller disclosure, in plain terms

{{img:0}}

A seller disclosure is a written statement from you about the home you are selling. It is separate from a buyer's inspection. An inspection shows what a professional finds on a given day. A disclosure records what you, the owner, know about the property.

In Tennessee, sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure, or an exemption form if the sale qualifies for one. Which one applies depends on the details of your sale, so check the current forms and rules with the Tennessee Real Estate Commission and ask a real estate attorney if you have a specific question.

A separate lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. We will get to that below.

The form matters most when it is finished early. If you hand it to your agent before the home is listed, buyers can read it alongside everything else when they are deciding whether to make an offer.

## The residential property condition disclosure

The condition disclosure asks about the home you have lived in or owned. Think of it as a walk through the house in writing: the roof, the plumbing, the heating and cooling, the foundation, past repairs, and anything else the form asks about.

A few habits make it go better:

- Fill it out yourself, from what you actually know. Do not guess and do not copy from an old form.
- Gather paperwork first: repair receipts, warranty documents, and records of past work.
- If you are unsure how to answer a question, ask before you write something down.
- If something changes between the day you fill it out and closing, tell your agent.

I cannot tell you how to answer a given question, and your agent cannot give legal advice either. What I can say is that the form works best when it is complete and consistent with what a buyer will later see in the home.

If you think your sale might qualify for an exemption, do not assume. Confirm it through the official sources or an attorney.

## The 1978 lead-based paint rule

{{img:1}}

Homes built before 1978 carry an extra requirement. For those homes, the lead-based paint disclosure applies, and it is its own item in the sale paperwork, separate from the condition disclosure.

The first step is simple: know the year your home was built. If you are not sure, ask your agent to help you confirm it. For Williamson County addresses, the [Williamson County property search](https://www.williamsoncounty-tn.gov/2099/35739/Property-Data-Search) is a place to start looking up your address. Keep in mind that counties differ. Spring Hill includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties, so the right county office depends on the address.

If your home was built in 1978 or later, this particular disclosure does not apply, though the condition disclosure or exemption still does.

If your home predates 1978, tell your agent early. That way the lead-based paint disclosure is ready when the contract is written instead of becoming a scramble. For questions about what the disclosure requires, go to the official sources, since I will not guess at details here.

## How disclosures fit with inspections

Disclosures and inspections do different jobs, and buyers often use both. A few items come up often:

- Termite and wood-destroying organism (WDO) inspections are commonly requested by buyers and lenders in Tennessee.
- Radon testing, a sewer scope and a termite inspection are common add-ons to a standard home inspection. The [EPA radon information](https://www.epa.gov/radon) page explains what radon is and how testing works.

If you know of an issue, it belongs on your disclosure whether or not an inspection would find it. If you do not know of one, an inspection may still turn something up, and that is normal. Sellers who have already read their own form tend to find an inspection report easier to understand, because they know what they wrote and why.

Some sellers choose to have repairs done or request their own inspection before listing. That is a choice, not a requirement, and it depends on the home and your budget. Your agent can talk through the options with you.

## A bit of market context

Market numbers do not change what goes on a disclosure, but they give you context for planning your sale. In Franklin, Redfin's rolling three-month data as of 2026-10-31 shows a median of 61 days on market and an average sale-to-list ratio of 97.9%. The same Redfin data shows 4.1 months of supply. Under the usual rule of thumb, 4 to 6 months of supply is considered balanced.

In Spring Hill, Redfin's rolling three-month data as of 2026-10-31 shows a median of 67 days on market and 4.5 months of supply. Those are city-wide figures, and they say nothing about any one house. If you want to see how your own area compares, the [Market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data) page is a good place to look.

For city-specific selling pages, see [Selling a home in Franklin](/franklin/selling-in-franklin) or [Selling a home in Spring Hill](/spring-hill/selling-in-spring-hill).

## Where to start

Here is a short order of operations:

1. Confirm the year your home was built.
2. Find the current forms through the Tennessee Real Estate Commission or your agent.
3. Collect repair records and warranties.
4. Complete the forms yourself, from what you know, and ask questions where you are unsure.

If you are thinking about selling and want to talk through the paperwork, start with [Find out what your home is worth](/sell#form) and I will follow up. We can walk through the disclosures, the timeline and what to expect, with no pressure.

faq.q: What is a Tennessee seller disclosure?
faq.a: It is a written statement from the seller about the home. In Tennessee, sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure, or an exemption if the sale qualifies. Check the Tennessee Real Estate Commission for current forms.

faq.q: Does the lead-based paint disclosure apply to every home?
faq.a: No. The lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. Confirm your home's year built and ask your agent how it affects your sale.

faq.q: Are disclosures the same as a home inspection?
faq.a: No. A disclosure is the seller's written statement about the home. An inspection is done by a professional. Buyers and lenders commonly request termite and wood-destroying organism inspections in Tennessee, and radon testing and a sewer scope are common add-ons.

faq.q: Where do I confirm which county my home is in?
faq.a: Check your address with the county. Spring Hill includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties, so county services, schools and taxes can differ by address.
